claim: PDZ domain scaffold proteins are molecular modules orchestrating cellular signalling in space and time.
source: PDZ domain scaffold proteins are molecular modules orchestrating cellular signalling in space and time.
evidence: This is a general statement from the abstract that draws on established scientific knowledge about PDZ domain scaffold proteins.

claim: Multivalent protein-protein and protein-lipid interactions provide critical avidity for the strong binding between the PDZ domain scaffold proteins, PICK1 and PSD-95, and their cognate transmembrane binding partners.
source: Our data demonstrate how multivalent protein-protein and protein-lipid interactions provide critical avidity for the strong binding between the PDZ domain scaffold proteins, PICK1 and PSD-95, and their cognate transmembrane binding partners.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript using SCMS assays.

claim: The kinetics of the binding between PICK1/PSD-95 and their transmembrane partners were remarkably slow.
source: The kinetics of the binding were remarkably slow and binding strength two-three orders of magnitude higher than the intrinsic affinity for the isolated PDZ interaction.
evidence: This is supported by kinetic experiments shown in the manuscript (e.g., Figure 3c-d).

claim: The binding strength between PICK1/PSD-95 and their transmembrane partners is two-three orders of magnitude higher than the intrinsic affinity for the isolated PDZ interaction.
source: The kinetics of the binding were remarkably slow and binding strength two-three orders of magnitude higher than the intrinsic affinity for the isolated PDZ interaction.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of SCMS binding data with in-solution fluorescence polarization assays.

claim: Discrete changes in the intrinsic PICK1 PDZ affinity did not affect overall binding strength but instead revealed dual scaffold modes for PICK1.
source: Interestingly, discrete changes in the intrinsic PICK1 PDZ affinity did not affect overall binding strength but instead revealed dual scaffold modes for PICK1.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing changes in Bmax rather than Kd* for different ligands (Figure 3).

claim: Intrinsic PDZ domain affinities are finely tuned and encode specific cellular responses, enabling multiplexed cellular functions of PDZ scaffolds.
source: Our data supported by simulations suggest that intrinsic PDZ domain affinities are finely tuned and encode specific cellular responses, enabling multiplexed cellular functions of PDZ scaffolds.
evidence: This is supported by both experimental data and mathematical modeling presented in the manuscript.

claim: Scaffold proteins play a key role in organizing signaling processes in space and time by operating as versatile nanoscale modules.
source: Scaffold proteins play a key role in these efforts by operating as versatile nanoscale modules capable of bringing distinct molecular components in close proximity to shape specificity in cellular signaling networks and regulate output (Good et al., 2011; Zeke et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Current understanding of the dynamics and kinetics underlying scaffold interactions relies mostly on in vitro assays of single domains isolated from their native membrane environment.
source: Our current understanding of the dynamics and kinetics underlying scaffold interactions relies mostly on in vitro assays of single domains isolated form their native membrane environment (Vincentelli et al., 2015; Stiffler et al., 2007; Long et al., 2003; Ivarsson, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature describing in vitro assays.

claim: In vitro measurements cannot replicate the behavior of scaffold proteins in the native environment due to the presence of several interaction domains and possible formation of higher order structures.
source: Nonetheless, the presence of several interaction domains in one protein, together with possible formation of higher order structures of both scaffold proteins and transmembrane interaction partners (Long et al., 2003; Ivarsson, 2012), strongly suggest that measurements in vitro cannot replicate the behavior of the native environment.
evidence: This is an inference based on known properties of scaffold proteins and supported by citations.

claim: Scaffold proteins often function on, or in proximity to, lipid cellular membranes.
source: Furthermore, scaffold proteins often function on, or in proximity, to lipid cellular membranes, and several scaffold protein domains directly interact with lipids (Egea-Jimenez et al., 2016; Pérez et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Several scaffold protein domains directly interact with lipids.
source: Furthermore, scaffold proteins often function on, or in proximity, to lipid cellular membranes, and several scaffold protein domains directly interact with lipids (Egea-Jimenez et al., 2016; Pérez et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: PDZ domains constitute one of the most common interaction domains in scaffold proteins.
source: PDZ (PSD-95/Discs Large/ZO-1) domains constitute one of the most common interaction domains in scaffold proteins (Feng and Zhang, 2009; Zhu et al., 2016; Ye and Zhang, 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: PDZ domains are characterized by an elongated binding groove that interacts with the last three to five C-terminal residues of the target proteins.
source: PDZ (PSD-95/Discs Large/ZO-1) domains constitute one of the most common interaction domains in scaffold proteins (Feng and Zhang, 2009; Zhu et al., 2016; Ye and Zhang, 2013) and are characterized by an elongated binding groove that interacts with the last three to five C-terminal residues of the target proteins (Doyle et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Scaffold proteins often contain several PDZ domains permitting them to serve as adaptors to assemble protein complexes.
source: Scaffold proteins often contain several PDZ domains permitting them to serve as adaptors to assemble protein complexes (Doyle et al., 1996; Sheng and Sala, 2001; Feng and Zhang, 2009; Ye and Zhang, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: PICK1 forms a dimeric structure containing two spatially separated, identical PDZ domains and a lipid binding N-BAR domain.
source: PICK1 (Protein Interacting with C Kinase 1), for example, forms a dimeric structure containing two spatially separated, identical PDZ domains and a lipid binding N-BAR (Bin/amphiphysin/Rvs) domain (Karlsen et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: PICK1 enables simultaneous binding of two interaction partners and tethering of the complex to the membrane.
source: PICK1 (Protein Interacting with C Kinase 1), for example, forms a dimeric structure containing two spatially separated, identical PDZ domains and a lipid binding N-BAR (Bin/amphiphysin/Rvs) domain (Karlsen et al., 2015), enabling simultaneous binding of two interaction partners and tethering of the complex to the membrane (Xu and Xia, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: PICK1 is believed to operate in two distinct modes of scaffolding: one required for clustering transmembrane interaction partners and one required for recruiting protein kinase Cα to its transmembrane interaction partners.
source: To perform its differential functions, PICK1 is believed to operate in two distinct modes of scaffolding; one required for clustering transmembrane interaction partners, such as the AMPA-type glutamate receptors (AMPARs), the metabotropic glutamate receptor 7 (mGluR7), ephrin and the monoamine transporters (Xia et al., 1999; Torres et al., 2001; Boudin et al., 2000; Torres et al., 1998), and one required for recruiting protein kinase Cα (PKCα) to its transmembrane interaction partners to regulate their phosphorylation (Baron et al., 2002; Dev et al., 2000; Perez et al., 2001; Staudinger et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The molecular mechanisms underlying the different scaffold modes of PICK1 remain unknown.
source: The molecular mechanisms underlying these different scaffold modes remain nevertheless unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field prior to this study.

claim: Drug-receptor or antibody interactions have been studied rigorously in tissues and cells uncovering molecular mechanisms of co-operativity and avidity.
source: In contrast to neuronal scaffold interactions, drug-receptor or antibody interactions have been studied rigorously in tissues and cells uncovering molecular mechanisms of co-operativity and avidity in many biological systems (Varner et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: SCMS are prepared by pressing a glass cover-slip on an adherent cell culture, and when the cover-slip is removed, the apical plasma membrane detaches from cells and a planar sheet exposing the inner surface of the membrane is exposed on the cover-slip.
source: SCMS are prepared by pressing a glass cover-slip on an adherent cell culture. When the cover-slip is removed, the apical plasma membrane detaches from cells and a planar sheet exposing the inner surface of the membrane is exposed on the cover-slip.
evidence: This describes the SCMS technique used in the study, based on previous work.

claim: Binding of fluorescence labeled protein ligands to the membrane proteins exposed on the SCMS can be quantified by confocal laser scanning microscopy.
source: Binding of fluorescence labeled protein ligands to the membrane proteins exposed on the SCMS can be quantified by confocal laser scanning microscopy.
evidence: This describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: The apparent affinity (Kd*) for PICK1 binding to SF-GluA2 on SCMS was 67 ± 6 nM.
source: The apparent affinity (Kd*) calculated from the binding curve was 67 ± 6 nM (mean ± s.e.m., n = 3)
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data from SCMS assays.

claim: The apparent affinity of PICK1 for SF-GluA2 on SCMS is ~100 fold higher than the low micromolar intrinsic affinity determined for binding of the GluA2 C-terminus to the PICK1 PDZ domain using an in-solution based assay.
source: The apparent affinity (Kd*) calculated from the binding curve was 67 ± 6 nM (mean ± s.e.m., n = 3), which, remarkably, is ~100 fold higher than the low micromolar intrinsic affinity (Kdint)determined for binding of the GluA2 C-terminus to the PICK1 PDZ domain using an in-solution based assay (Erlendsson et al., 2014).
evidence: This compares experimental data from SCMS with previously published in-solution data.

claim: Adding an alanine residue to the GluA2 C-terminus (-ESVKI + A) compromises PDZ ligand binding.
source: To test if the observed binding was specific and dependent on the C-terminal PDZ binding motif (-ESVKI) in GluA2, we added an alanine residue to the GluA2 C-terminus (-ESVKI + A) (SF-GluA2 +A) to compromise PDZ ligand binding (Madsen et al., 2005; Madsen et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature and experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: The apparent affinity and the maximal binding (Bmax) of PICK1 were significantly reduced for SF-GluA2 +A compared to binding to SF-GluA2 for similar receptor expression levels.
source: The apparent affinity and the maximal binding (Bmax) of PICK1 were significantly reduced compared to binding to SF-GluA2 for similar receptor expression levels (Figure 1b,e,f).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: PICK1 binding to SCMS from GluA2 expressing cells is specific and depends on the interaction with the GluA2 C-terminal PDZ motif.
source: This supports that PICK1 binding to SCMS from GluA2 expressing cells is specific and depends on the interaction with the GluA2 C-terminal PDZ motif.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing reduced binding with the +A mutation.

claim: The Kd* for PICK1 binding to TAC-YFP-GluA2 was 73 ± 19 nM.
source: Strikingly, we obtained a Kd* of 73 ± 19 nM (mean ±s.e.m., n = 3) for binding of PICK1 to TAC-YFP-GluA2 (Figure 1h,i)
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data from SCMS assays.

claim: The high apparent affinity of PICK1 for membrane-embedded ligands is achieved independently of the tetrameric complex of AMPARs.
source: Strikingly, we obtained a Kd* of 73 ± 19 nM (mean ±s.e.m., n = 3) for binding of PICK1 to TAC-YFP-GluA2 (Figure 1h,i) suggesting that the high apparent affinity was achieved independently of the tetrameric complex as well as of the membrane embedded segments of the receptor.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing similar Kd* for TAC-YFP-GluA2 (monomeric) and SF-GluA2 (tetrameric).

claim: The high apparent affinity of PICK1 for membrane-embedded ligands is achieved independently of the membrane embedded segments of the receptor.
source: Strikingly, we obtained a Kd* of 73 ± 19 nM (mean ±s.e.m., n = 3) for binding of PICK1 to TAC-YFP-GluA2 (Figure 1h,i) suggesting that the high apparent affinity was achieved independently of the tetrameric complex as well as of the membrane embedded segments of the receptor.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data using TAC constructs.

claim: The DAT C-terminus has a 10-fold higher intrinsic affinity for PICK1 than the GluA2 peptide according to in-solution binding assays.
source: According to in-solution binding assays, this peptide has a 10-fold higher intrinsic affinity for PICK1 than the GluA2 peptide (Erlendsson et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The Kd* for PICK1 binding to TAC-YFP-DAT C24 was 47 ± 5 nM.
source: We observed specific binding also for this construct (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) but only a minor increase in Kd* (47 ± 5 nM, mean ±s.e.m., n = 7)
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data from SCMS assays.

claim: The binding strength measured in the SCMS assay correlates poorly with the intrinsic affinity.
source: We observed specific binding also for this construct (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) but only a minor increase in Kd* (47 ± 5 nM, mean ±s.e.m., n = 7), revealing that the binding strength measured in the SCMS assay correlates poorly with the intrinsic affinity (Figure 1a,c).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing SCMS data with in-solution affinity data.

claim: The Ki* for PICK1 binding to TAC-YFP-DAT determined from competition binding was 29 ± 5 nM.
source: The binding strength determined from competition binding (Ki*=29 ± 5 nM (mean ±s.e.m., n = 5) was close to that from the direct binding saturation assay
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data from competition binding assays on SCMS.

claim: The binding strength of PICK1 for TAC-YFP-DAT on SCMS is increased 100-fold compared to the intrinsic affinity of the PICK1 PDZ interaction with the DAT C-terminus obtained in solution.
source: The binding strength determined from competition binding (Ki*=29 ± 5 nM (mean ±s.e.m., n = 5) was close to that from the direct binding saturation assay and increased 100-fold compared to the intrinsic affinity of the PICK1 PDZ interaction with the DAT C-terminus obtained in solution using a fluorescence polarization competition assay (2.1 ± 0.4 μM) (Figure 2b,d).
evidence: This compares experimental data from SCMS with in-solution fluorescence polarization data.

claim: The measured binding strength of PSD-95 PDZ 1–2 tandem domain on SCMS expressing the ß1-adrenergic receptor was EC50 = 3 ± 2 μM.
source: Indeed, the measured binding strength (EC50 = 3 ± 2 μM) was two orders of magnitude increased compared to the intrinsic affinities previously measured in solution for either of the two domains (430 ± 47 µM and 120 ± 20 µM for PDZ1 and PDZ2, respectively) (Møller et al., 2013) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2a,b).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data from SCMS assays.

claim: The binding strength of PSD-95 PDZ 1–2 on SCMS was two orders of magnitude increased compared to the intrinsic affinities previously measured in solution for either of the two domains.
source: Indeed, the measured binding strength (EC50 = 3 ± 2 μM) was two orders of magnitude increased compared to the intrinsic affinities previously measured in solution for either of the two domains (430 ± 47 µM and 120 ± 20 µM for PDZ1 and PDZ2, respectively) (Møller et al., 2013) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2a,b).
evidence: This compares experimental data from SCMS with previously published in-solution data.

claim: The binding strengths of PDZ domain scaffolding interactions are substantially higher than intrinsic PDZ affinities.
source: These findings further support that the binding strengths of PDZ domain scaffolding interactions are substantially higher than intrinsic PDZ affinities.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data for both PICK1 and PSD-95.

claim: There is a two-fold difference in total maximal binding (Bmax) between PICK1 binding to TAC-YFP-GluA2 and TAC-YFP-DAT.
source: Despite similar high binding strength, comparison of the binding curves for PICK1 binding to TAC-YFP-GluA2 and TAC-YFP-DAT revealed a surprising two-fold difference in total maximal binding (Bmax) (TAC-YFP-DAT Bmax = 100%; TAC-YFP-GluA2 Bmax = 44 ± 9%) (Figure 2—figure supplement 3a,b).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data from SCMS assays.

claim: The intrinsic affinity of PICK1 for the DAT C-terminus depends on the C-terminal valine and substitution of the aliphatic side-chain of the C-terminal valine decreases its intrinsic affinity for PICK1 in the order Val (WT) (2.3 ± 0.1 µM)>Ile (9.5 ± 0.9 µM)>Ala (49 ± 3 µM).
source: To address whether the difference was a consequence of the different intrinsic affinities of the DAT C-terminus compared to the GluA2 C-terminus, we exploited that the intrinsic affinity of PICK1 for the DAT C-terminus depends on the C-terminal valine and that substitution of the aliphatic side-chain of the C-terminal valine decrease its intrinsic affinity for PICK1; Val (WT) (2.3 ± 0.1 µM)>Ile (9.5 ± 0.9 µM)>Ala (49 ± 3 µM) (Madsen et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The apparent affinity of PICK1 to LKV (Kd*=37 ± 5 nM) was essentially the same as that seen for TAC-YFP-DAT.
source: The apparent affinity of PICK1 to LKV (Kd*=37 ± 5 nM, n = 8) (mean ±s.e.m.) (Figure 3a,b) was essentially the same as that seen for TAC-YFP-DAT (Figure 2).
evidence: This compares experimental data from SCMS assays for different constructs.

claim: Despite a decrease in intrinsic affinity of up to >20 fold, no differences in apparent affinity in the SCMS assay were observed upon mutating the valine to isoleucine (LKI Kd*=39 ± 4 nM) or alanine (LKA Kd*=59 ± 11 nM).
source: Moreover, despite a decrease in intrinsic affinity of up to >20 fold, we observed no differences in apparent affinity in the SCMS assay upon mutating the valine to isoleucine (LKI Kd*=39 ± 4 nM, n = 7) or alanine (LKA Kd*=59 ± 11 nM, n = 5) (Figure 3a,b).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data from SCMS assays.

claim: An unexpected reduction in maximal binding (Bmax) was observed for LKI (56 ± 2%) and LKA (41 ± 4%) relative to LKV for similar receptor surface expression levels.
source: Instead, we observed an unexpected reduction in maximal binding (Bmax LKI: 56 ± 2%, LKA: 41 ± 4%; (means ±s.e.m.) relative to LKV (Figure 3a,b and Table 1) for similar receptor surface expression levels (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data from SCMS assays.

claim: Association experiments did not show any striking difference between LKV and LKI.
source: Association experiments did not show any striking difference between LKV and LKI (Figure 3c–d).
evidence: This is based on kinetic experimental data shown in Figure 3c-d.

claim: Both LKV and LKI displayed slow (half-bound maxima; LKV: 24 ± 8 min, LKI: 14 ± 6 min), but saturable binding.
source: Both constructs displayed slow (half-bound maxima; LKV: 24 ± 8 min, LKI: 14 ± 6 min; (means ±s.e.m., n = 3)), but saturable binding.
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data from kinetic assays.

claim: PICK1 dissociated very slowly when bound to LKI (t½=431 ± 16 min).
source: PICK1 dissociation, on the other hand, revealed that whereas PICK dissociated very slowly when bound to LKI (t½=431 ± 16 min; mean ±s.e.m., n = 3)
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data from dissociation assays.

claim: A distinct fast component of dissociation was observed from LKV on top of the slow dissociation rate (t½=21 ± 8 and 373 ± 51 min).
source: PICK1 dissociation, on the other hand, revealed that whereas PICK dissociated very slowly when bound to LKI (t½=431 ± 16 min; mean ±s.e.m., n = 3), a distinct fast component of dissociation was observed from LKV on top of the slow dissociation rate (t½=21 ± 8 and 373 ± 51 min; mean ±s.e.m., n = 3), (Figure 3e–f).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data from dissociation assays.

claim: The unbinding of LKV consists of two kinetically distinct processes suggesting that PICK1 might engage in two different binding configurations depending on the concentration of PICK1 and the intrinsic affinity for the membrane embedded ligand.
source: This suggests that the unbinding of LKV consists of two kinetically distinct processes and that PICK1 therefore might engage in two different binding configurations depending on the concentration of PICK1 and the intrinsic affinity for the membrane embedded ligand.
evidence: This is an inference based on the dissociation kinetics data.

claim: When the concentration of PICK1 is low and the intrinsic affinity for the membrane embedded ligand is low, PICK1 might adopt the binding mode with both PDZ domains of the dimer bound to a membrane embedded ligand (slow dissociation rate).
source: That is, when the concentration of PICK1 is low and the intrinsic affinity for the membrane embedded ligand is low, PICK1 might adopt the intuitive binding mode with both PDZ domains of the dimer bound to a membrane embedded ligand (slow dissociation rate).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the experimental data and kinetic modeling.

claim: When the concentration of PICK1 is high and the intrinsic affinity for the membrane embedded ligand is high, PICK1 might gradually switch to a binding mode with only one PDZ domain engaged in binding of the membrane embedded ligand (fast dissociation rate).
source: However, when the concentration of PICK1 is high and the intrinsic affinity for the membrane embedded ligand is high, PICK1 might gradually switch to a binding mode with only one PDZ domain engaged in binding of the membrane embedded ligand (fast dissociation rate).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the experimental data and kinetic modeling.

claim: Bivalency increases the overall affinity and residence time since this permits multiple partial unbinding and rebinding events to take place before the protein fully dissociates.
source: Indeed, bivalency increases the overall affinity and residence time since this permits multiple partial unbinding and rebinding events to take place before the protein fully dissociates (Vauquelin and Charlton, 2013; Vauquelin and Charlton, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: When the bulk concentration of PICK1 is sufficiently high, the free bivalent PICK1 would be expected to outpace binding of the second PDZ domain, thereby preventing formation of the bivalently bound complex and instead leading to formation of the ternary complex.
source: However, when the bulk concentration of PICK1 [aa] is sufficiently high, the free bivalent PICK1 would be expected to outpace binding of the second PDZ domain, thereby preventing formation of the 'red complex' (aAAa) and instead leading to formation of the 'blue complex' (aaAAaa) (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is based on thermodynamic modeling and simulations.

claim: By simultaneously solving the system of differential equations related to formation of all of the involved complexes, a biphasic saturation binding curve was obtained that overall was in good agreement with the experimentally derived saturation binding curve observed for PICK1 binding to LKV.
source: By simultaneously solving the system of differential equations related to formation of all of the involved complexes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a–b), and using k1 and k-1 values derived of from the in-solution PDZ binding to soluble ligands (Erlendsson and Madsen, 2015; Erlendsson et al., 2014) together with an inter PDZ distance (r) of 180 Å determined from the structure of PICK1 based on Small-Angle X-ray Scattering (Karlsen et al., 2015)) and an f value of 185, we obtained a biphasic saturation binding curve (Figure 4b) that overall was in good agreement with the experimentally derived saturation binding curve observed for PICK1 binding to LKV.
evidence: This is based on mathematical modeling using parameters from experimental data and literature.

claim: The biphasic shape of the saturation binding curve results from the population of the ternary blue complex (aaAAaa) outpacing the binary red complex (aAAa) at concentrations above 100 nM of PICK1.
source: Importantly, the biphasic shape results from the population of the ternary blue complex (aaAAaa) outpacing the binary red complex (aAAa) at concentrations above 100 nM of PICK1.
evidence: This is based on the results of the mathematical modeling.

claim: The simulations are in very good agreement with the actual dissociation experiment.
source: Importantly, the simulations are in very good agreement with the actual dissociation experiment (Figure 3e,f).
evidence: This compares simulation results with experimental data.

claim: The model predicts that no differences in the apparent maximal binding should be observed for the different ligands if one of the PDZ domains is rendered non-functional.
source: The model described above and in Figure 4 relies on two independent PDZ domain ligand-binding sites in the PICK1 dimer, and consequently it predicts that no differences in the apparent maximal binding should be observed for the different ligands if one of the PDZ domains is rendered non-functional.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the mathematical model.

claim: PICK1 A87L binds very weakly to SCMSs.
source: We found that PICK1 A87L bind very weakly also to SCMSs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data from SCMS assays.

claim: PICK1 WT/WT binding to LKV revealed a two-fold higher Bmax than for LKI with no difference in binding strength.
source: Importantly, PICK1 WT/WT binding to LKV revealed again a two-fold higher Bmax than for LKI with no difference in binding strength (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data from SCMS assays with homodimers.

claim: No difference in Bmax between LKV and LKI was observed for the PICK1 WT/A87L heterodimers, demonstrating that the difference in Bmax must rely on PDZ domain bivalency.
source: In agreement with our model, we did no longer observe any difference in Bmax between LKV and LKI for the PICK1 WT/A87L heterodimers, demonstrating that the difference in Bmax indeed must rely on PDZ domain bivalency (Figure 5d,e).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data from SCMS assays with heterodimers.

claim: The resulting binding curves for LKV showed a binding strength similar to that of the PICK1 WT homodimers (WT/WT Kd*=37 ± 5 nM; WT/A87L Kd*=24 ± 21 nM), suggesting that one PDZ domain is sufficient to support the strong binding and corroboration of the ternary complex binding mode.
source: Moreover, the resulting binding curves for LKV showed a binding strength similar to that of the PICK1 WT homodimers (WT/WT Kd*=37 ± 5 nM; WT/A87L Kd*=24 ± 21 nM, mean ±s.e.m., n = 3) (Figure 5d,e), suggesting that one PDZ domain is sufficient to support the strong binding and corroboration of the ternary complex binding mode (blue complex in Figure 4a).
evidence: This is based on experimental data from SCMS assays and supports the model.

claim: For LKI, a significant decrease in the apparent affinity of PICK1 WT/A87L heterodimers was observed in both channels (WT/WT Kd* *=29 ± 4 nM, WT/A87L Kd*=123 ± 41 nM), suggesting that the high binding strength observed for WT/WT does rely on the dual PDZ domains.
source: For LKI, however, we observed a significant decrease in the apparent affinity of PICK1 WT/A87L heterodimers in both channels (WT/WT Kd* *=29 ± 4 nM, WT/A87L Kd*=123 ± 41 nM, mean ±s.e.m., n = 3) (Figure 5d,e), suggesting that the high binding strength observed for WT/WT does rely on the dual PDZ domains in agreement with the model.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from SCMS assays and supports the model.

claim: One PICK1 WT/WT dimer preferentially binds one membrane embedded LKV ligand (i.e. with 1:1 stoichiometry).
source: Altogether, these findings strongly support a 'dual scaffold mode' as outlined in our model and simulations above; that is, one PICK1 WT/WT dimer preferentially binds one membrane embedded LKV ligand (i.e. with 1:1 stoichiometry).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data and modeling.

claim: One PICK1 WT/WT dimer preferentially binds two membrane embedded LKI ligands (i.e. with 1:2 stoichiometry), thereby preserving a high binding strength due to the avidity obtained by doubling the PDZ interactions.
source: In contrast, one PICK1 WT/WT dimer preferentially binds two membrane embedded LKI ligands (i.e. with 1:2 stoichiometry), thereby preserving a high binding strength due to the avidity obtained by doubling the PDZ interactions.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data and modeling.

claim: Upon compromising the PDZ bivalence (PICK1WT/A87L), PICK1 is forced to obtain the 1:1 configuration, which increases Bmax at the expense of binding strength for LKI.
source: Upon compromising the PDZ bivalence (PICK1WT/A87L), however, PICK1 is forced to obtain the 1:1 configuration, which increase Bmax at the expense of binding strength for LKI (Figure 5f).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data and modeling.

claim: Expression of eYFP-PICK1 did not affect the isoproterenol-induced internalization of any of the constructs.
source: Expression of eYFP-PICK1 did not affect the isoproterenol-induced internalization of any of the constructs (Figure 5g)
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data from surface ELISA assays.

claim: Expression of eYFP-PICK1 significantly inhibited the reinsertion into the plasma membrane of LKV normalized to LKV +A after alprenolol treatment (41.5 ± 12% vs 100%).
source: however, expression significantly inhibited the reinsertion into the plasma membrane of LKV normalized to LKV +A after alprenolol treatment (41.5 ± 12% vs 100%, mean ±s.e.m., n = 6) as previously described (Madsen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data from surface ELISA assays.

claim: eYFP-PICK1 expression did not significantly affect the reinsertion of either LKI or LKA (88.8 ± 14% and 95.9 ± 3.9%, respectively).
source: In contrast, eYFP-PICK1 expression did not significantly affect the reinsertion of either LKI or LKA (88.8 ± 14% and 95.9 ± 3.9%, respectively, mean ±s.e.m., n = 6) (Figure 5h)
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data from surface ELISA assays.

claim: The ability of PICK1 to reduce recycling of an interaction partner could be dependent on formation of the ternary (blue) complex and hence the ability to recruit for example kinases.
source: This suggests that the ability of PICK1 to reduce recycling of an interaction partner could be dependent on formation of the ternary (blue) complex and hence the ability to recruit for example kinases (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is an inference based on the functional data and the binding model.

claim: PICK1 V121E,L125E showed markedly reduced binding strength for the LKV (PICK1 V121E,L125E, Kd*=286 ± 126 nM) on SCMSs compared to PICK1 WT without affecting maximal binding.
source: PICK1 V121E,L125E showed markedly reduced binding strength for the LKV (PICK1 V121E,L125E, Kd*=286 ± 126 nM, mean ± s.e.m., n = 3) on SCMSs compared to PICK1 WT without affecting maximal binding (Figure 6b and Table 3).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data from SCMS assays.

claim: The binding strength of the PICK1 WT relies in part on membrane binding.
source: This supports that the binding strength of the PICK1 WT relies in part on membrane binding.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data with the amphipathic helix mutant.

claim: Expression of eYFP-PICK1 V121E,L125E reduced the reinsertion of LKV significantly (+Tet 50.9 ± 8.3% vs –Tet 86.0 ± 13%) and to the same extent as eYFP-PICK1 WT (+Tet 51.3 ± 3.1 vs –Tet 81.7 ± 7.7).
source: Expression of eYFP-PICK1 V121E,L125E reduced the reinsertion of LKV significantly (+Tet 50.9 ± 8.3% vs –Tet 86.0 ± 13%, mean ±s.e.m., n = 6) and to the same extend as eYFP-PICK1 WT (+Tet 51.3 ± 3.1 vs –Tet 81.7 ± 7.7, mean ±s.e.m., n = 6) (Figure 6c–d)
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data from surface ELISA assays.

claim: The function of PICK1 in regulating receptor recycling is independent of the avidity provided by the membrane binding helix, but instead relies on a sufficiently high PICK1 concentration to achieve formation of 1:1 configuration.
source: suggesting that this function of PICK1 is independent on the avidity provided by the membrane binding helix, but instead relies on a sufficiently high PICK1 concentration to achieve formation of 1:1 configuration (Figure 4, blue).
evidence: This is an inference based on the functional data with the amphipathic helix mutant.

claim: GFP-PICK1 WT showed partial clustering and significant localization to dendritic spines, which was reflected in a high level of co-clustering with the synaptic marker PSD-95.
source: Similarly, to endogenous PICK1, virally expressed GFP-PICK1 WT showed partial clustering and significant localization to dendritic spines, which was reflected in a high level of co-clustering with the synaptic marker PSD-95 (Figure 6f, colocalization shown in white in merged picture).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data from confocal imaging of hippocampal neurons.

claim: GFP-PICK1 V121E,L125E had similar levels of expression in somatic regions (101 ± 8% of wt, p=0.94, n = 16).
source: GFP-PICK1 V121E,L125E had similar levels of expression in somatic regions (101 ± 8% of wt, p=0.94, n = 16) (Figure 6g)
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data from confocal imaging of hippocampal neurons.

claim: GFP-PICK1 V121E,L125E distributed much less into the dendrites and displayed a more diffuse localization than GFP-PICK1 WT.
source: GFP-PICK1 V121E,L125E had similar levels of expression in somatic regions (101 ± 8% of wt, p=0.94, n = 16) (Figure 6g), but distributed much less into the dendrites and displayed a more diffuse localization than GFP-PICK1 WT.
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data from confocal imaging of hippocampal neurons.

claim: The total number of GFP-PICK1 V121E,L125E clusters relative to PSD-95 clusters was significantly reduced compared to GFP-PICK1WT (48.5 ± 7% of GFP-PICK1 WT, p<0.0001, n = 24).
source: The total number of GFP-PICK1 V121E,L125E clusters relative to PSD-95 clusters was significantly reduced compared to GFP-PICK1WT (48.5 ± 7% of GFP-PICK1 WT, p<0.0001, n = 24) (Figure 6h)
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data from confocal imaging of hippocampal neurons.

claim: The number of PSD-95 clusters per length of dendrite was unchanged (97 ± 10%, p=0.81, n = 24).
source: whereas the number of PSD-95 clusters per length of dendrite was unchanged (97 ± 10%, p=0.81, n = 24) (Figure 6i).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data from confocal imaging of hippocampal neurons.

claim: The localization to dendritic spines and consequently the co-clustering of GFP-PICK1 V121E,L125E with PSD-95 was almost abolished compared to GFP-PICK1 WT (0.17 ± 0.04, p<0.0001, n = 24).
source: Interestingly, the localization to dendritic spines and consequently the co-clustering of GFP-PICK1 V121E,L125E with PSD-95 was almost abolished compared to GFP-PICK1 WT (0.17 ± 0.04, p<0.0001, n = 24) (Figure 6j)
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data from confocal imaging of hippocampal neurons.

claim: The binding strength provided by the membrane binding capability of the amphipathic helix is essential for stable synaptic localization of PICK1.
source: This demonstrates that the binding strength provided by the membrane binding capability of the amphipathic helix is essential for stable synaptic localization of PICK1.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the neuronal localization data.

claim: As a result of the avidity of multiple protein-protein and/or protein-lipid interactions, the two PDZ scaffold proteins PICK1 and PSD-95 both displayed binding strength several orders of magnitude higher than the intrinsic affinities for individual PDZ interactions.
source: As a result of the avidity of multiple protein-protein and/or protein-lipid interactions, the two PDZ scaffold proteins PICK1 and PSD-95 both displayed binding strength several orders of magnitude higher than the intrinsic affinities for individual PDZ interactions (see Tables 1–3).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the experimental data presented.

claim: PICK1 binds native membrane proteins in the SCMS using the PDZ domain.
source: These findings have two implications: 1) PICK1 binds native membrane proteins in the SCMS using the PDZ domain
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing reduced binding with PDZ mutations.

claim: PICK1 does not bind the membrane in absence of PDZ interactions.
source: These findings have two implications: 1) PICK1 binds native membrane proteins in the SCMS using the PDZ domain and 2) PICK1 does not bind the membrane in absence of PDZ interactions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing no binding of A87L mutant.

claim: Disruption of the membrane binding amphipathic helix in PICK1 reduced the affinity of the interaction.
source: Disruption of the membrane binding amphipathic helix in PICK1 reduced the affinity of the interaction (Figure 6b), suggesting that the interaction with the membrane does play a role in context of the PDZ binding.
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data from SCMS assays.

claim: The high binding strength in the SCMSs implies that often scaffold proteins may be at saturating concentrations in vivo – in particular given high local concentrations of transmembrane interaction partners.
source: Regardless the molecular explanation of the high binding strength in the SCMSs, it implies that often scaffold proteins may be at saturating concentrations in vivo – in particular given high local concentrations of transmembrane interaction partners.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing nanomolar binding strengths.

claim: Tuning of affinities/avidities may represent a relatively inefficient mechanism of regulation.
source: Tuning of affinities/avidities may therefore represent a relative inefficient mechanism of regulation, which we importantly could demonstrate by the ability of mutant PICK1 (PICK1V121E,L125E) to retain cellular function despite a ten-fold drop in binding strength according to the SCMS assay.
evidence: This is an inference based on the functional data with the amphipathic helix mutant.

claim: The slow binding kinetics observed for PICK1 imply that the scaffold interactions that underlie biological regulation are likely to occur under non-equilibrium conditions.
source: The slow binding kinetics observed for PICK1, on the other hand, imply that the scaffold interactions that underlie biological regulation are likely to occur under non-equilibrium conditions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the kinetic data.

claim: Factors affecting the binding kinetics (e.g. sterical hindrance and flexibility) may have hitherto unappreciated biological impact.
source: Consequently, factors affecting the binding kinetics (e.g. sterical hindrance and flexibility) may have hitherto unappreciated biological impact.
evidence: This is speculation based on the kinetic data and modeling.

claim: The slow off-rates observed for PICK1 provide a putative biological mechanism to convert a transient signal into a long-lived effect.
source: The slow off-rates observed for PICK1 moreover provide a putative biological mechanism to convert at transient signal (such as an activity dependent exposure of the GluA2 C-terminus) into a long-lived effect (e.g. membrane localization of PICK1).
evidence: This is speculation based on the kinetic data.

claim: The behavior of PICK1 reflects an affinity dependent switch in the scaffolding mode of PICK1 – that is, using both PDZ domains for interacting with membrane associated PDZ partners with low intrinsic affinity, but only one PDZ domain when the local bulk concentration is above or close to the intrinsic affinity.
source: Instead, our kinetic modeling together with the experimental data suggests that this behavior reflects an affinity dependent switch in the scaffolding mode of PICK1 – that is, using both PDZ domains for interacting with membrane associated PDZ partners with low intrinsic affinity, but only one PDZ domain when the local bulk concentration is above or close to the intrinsic affinity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data and mathematical modeling.

claim: After binding to the first binding site, penalties associated with binding of the second site of the bivalent interaction may rather favor binding of a second molecule from the solution.
source: Thus, after binding to the first binding site penalties associated with binding of the second site of the bivalent interaction (e.g. from reduced entropy, straining of the molecule and steric hindrance) may rather favor binding of a second molecule from the solution (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is based on kinetic simulations and supported by citations.

claim: The behavior of PICK1 is likely favored by the large distance (~20 nm) between the two PDZ domains in PICK1, which will render the effective local concentration of the second PDZ domain after binding of the first relatively low.
source: Importantly, this behavior is likely favored by the large distance (~20 nm) between the two PDZ domains in PICK1 (Karlsen et al., 2015), which will render the effective local concentration, [L], of the second PDZ domain after binding of the first relatively low compared to for example the tandem domains in PSD95.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural data and the modeling.

claim: The scaffolding mode for high intrinsic affinity ligands (including DAT and NET) would leave one PDZ domain free for recruitment of cytosolic proteins (e.g. kinases, phosphatases, GTPases).
source: Functionally, the scaffolding mode for high intrinsic affinity ligands (including DAT and NET) (Erlendsson et al., 2014) would leave one PDZ domain free for recruitment of cytosolic proteins (e.g. kinases, phosphatases, GTPases).
evidence: This is an inference based on the binding model and functional data.

claim: Only the scaffolding mode with one free PDZ domain supports the PICK1 function in regulating recycling of the β2AR.
source: Only this mode supports the PICK1 function in regulating recycling of the β2AR.
evidence: This is based on the functional data showing differential effects on recycling.

claim: For ligands with lower intrinsic affinity (including GluA2, ASIC1a, HER2, Glt1b, mGluR7b and Ephrin B1), both PDZ domains would be engaged with membrane-associated ligands.
source: For ligands with lower intrinsic affinity (including GluA2, ASIC1a, HER2, Glt1b, mGluR7b and Ephrin B1) (Erlendsson et al., 2014), however, both PDZ domains would be engaged with membrane-associated ligands.
evidence: This is an inference based on the binding model.

claim: The scaffold mode with both PDZ domains engaged will potentially lead to clustering of the ligands and possibly changes in lateral diffusion, rotational flexibility, and molecular orientation.
source: This scaffold mode will potentially lead to clustering of the ligands and possibly changes in lateral diffusion, rotational flexibility, and molecular orientation - including positioning of the C-terminus relative to the membrane.
evidence: This is speculation based on the binding model.

claim: The PICK1 N-BAR domain is recruited to biological membranes in a curvature sensitive manner.
source: Finally, since the PICK1 N-BAR domain, like other N-BAR proteins, is recruited to biological membranes in a curvature sensitive manner (Herlo et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The PICK1 concentration on membranes might be almost two orders of magnitude higher in areas of high curvature such as endocytic structures, endosomes or vesicles in the biosynthetic pathway.
source: the PICK1 concentration on membranes might be almost two orders of magnitude higher in areas of high curvature such as endocytic structures, endosomes or vesicles in the biosynthetic pathway (Bhatia et al., 2009).
evidence: This is speculation based on known properties of N-BAR domains and supported by a citation.
